metadata.file_name: 99. Jiao et al. (2021). Editorial: Process Data in Educational and Psychological Measurement.pdf
metadata.title: Editorial: Process Data in Educational and Psychological Measurement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This editorial does not conduct a new empirical analysis of ILSA microdata; instead, it summarizes and contextualizes a research topic containing multiple studies. Because no analytic dataset, sampling frame, or estimation procedure is implemented here, there are no student-level sampling weights or replicate-weight schemes to report. For readers applying the cited studies, the appropriate ILSA weight variables (e.g., student design weights and BRR/JRR replicate weights when provided by the data producer) should be used when estimating population-representative statistics and standard errors. Plausible values (when used in the underlying achievement-focused studies) should be combined using the assessment’s standard PV methodology (e.g., Rubin’s rules) rather than treating PVs as single imputed scores.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This piece is an editorial that does not analyze student achievement outcomes from ILSA instruments and therefore does not generate or model plausible values. The plausible-values framework is relevant to the underlying empirical papers it summarizes, but it is not applied within this editorial’s own methods. As a result, PV handling is not applicable to the editorial itself, and missing-data handling is not reported because no dataset is analyzed here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic sample is defined in this editorial. It provides an overview of papers in a research topic and does not specify inclusion/exclusion criteria, grade/domain subsamples, or any student-level dataset construction steps.

data.outcome_summary: This editorial does not present original empirical results, model estimates, or performance metrics. Instead, it provides an overview of research directions and example papers that use educational and psychological process data (e.g., response processes, response times, sequence patterns, and collaborative problem-solving traces) across multiple large-scale assessment contexts such as PISA and PIAAC. The table of collected papers highlights a range of statistical and machine-learning approaches (including hidden Markov modeling, sequence mining, and supervised ML comparisons) used in the underlying studies, but those methods are not executed or evaluated within this editorial. Consequently, there are no benchmarks, effect sizes, or predictive accuracy measures attributable to this article itself. The main contribution is conceptual and methodological signposting for how process data can be leveraged in measurement research, rather than evidence for a specific policy intervention derived from this paper’s own analysis.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a journal editorial rather than an empirical study or a technical report. As such, it does not define an ILSA dataset/cycle, does not specify an analytic sample, and does not train or evaluate ML models with reported metrics. The absence of main findings, confounders, and sample details is therefore expected given the article type and its role as a curated overview of a research topic.
